idiom_name: per-instance extension registry (Map<Class<?>, Object> + getExtension) or a WeakHashMap side table
implementation_notes: Java has neither extension members nor a way to add fields to a foreign class, so the structure is hand-written: the key abstraction (or an interface it implements, such as Extensible) exposes <T> T getExtension(Class<T> type), backed by a Map<Class<?>, Object> keyed by the extension interface's Class object - the class token is Java's equivalent of Gamma's typeid-based extension identity - with type.cast(...) on the way out and null (or Optional) when the capability is absent. Where the subject cannot be touched at all, the registry moves outside it into a java.util.WeakHashMap keyed by the instance: its documentation notes that keys are held indirectly and that the map works best with keys whose equals tests identity, while values must not strongly reference their own keys. Dominant frameworks package the same structure, with adapters in the extension role: Eclipse's IAdaptable.getAdapter plus the IAdapterManager registry of IAdapterFactory instances (registerable programmatically or declaratively through the org.eclipse.core.runtime.adapters extension point) is the canonical Java instance of the pattern, and Swing's JComponent client properties are a per-component attribute bag of the same shape.
pitfalls: WeakHashMap holds keys weakly but values strongly: an extension that references its subject keeps the entry (and therefore the subject) alive forever - store state that does not point back at the key, or wrap values in WeakReference.

WeakHashMap's size, keySet and entrySet shrink asynchronously as the collector runs, so iteration is not stable and cannot be used for deterministic cleanup; the class is also not synchronised, and composite operations race under concurrent attachment.

A null return turns a missing capability into a NullPointerException a long way from the query - return Optional<T> or document the absence, and keep the class token and payload type in sync or the ClassCastException surfaces at the cast.

Hand-written registries need a policy for replacement and removal: put() silently overwrites (an extension can be replaced by a component that should not have that right), and a HashMap keyed by an interface Class collides with inherited extension interfaces unless the lookup walks the supertype hierarchy the way IAdapterManager does.
